title: Bat flight arose from an apparatus for gliding

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Bat flight arose from an apparatus for gliding

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Bats were derived from gliding animals, and the wing membrane extending to the tail and hind legs in some bats is a trace of an apparatus originally built for gliding rather than flight.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In bats which have the wing-membrane extended from the top of the shoulder to the tail, including the hind-legs, we perhaps see traces of an apparatus originally constructed for gliding through the air rather than for flight.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VI, “Difficulties on Theory”; section “Transitions in habits of life.”. Scope: bats and gliding mammals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch06-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public fossil and morphology resources permit explicit ancestral-state analyses. The critical transition is poorly sampled, so existing data can constrain but not decisively recover the origin of bat flight.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct bat ancestry using fossil-calibrated mammal phylogenies and compare ancestral forelimb and membrane characters with extant and fossil gliders. Transitional gliding-adapted anatomy predating powered-flight characters supports the claim; evidence for a non-gliding ancestor or alternative functional sequence refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The earliest known bats were already capable of powered flight.

Soft flight membranes are rarely preserved and extant gliders are not necessarily ancestral analogues.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Ordinal relationships and the earliest bat fossils are public, and a standard tree would show whether bats are derived from any living gliding mammal group. That test is decisive against a pathway through colugos or flying squirrels and does not exhaust an unknown extinct gliding stage. The functional reading of the wing membrane as a trace of gliding remains an inference from limited fossils.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place bats, colugos, and gliding rodents on a phylogeny and score the locomotor apparatus of the earliest fossil bats. Nesting of bats among gliding mammals, or early fossils built for gliding rather than flapping, would support derivation from a gliding apparatus; non-gliding nearest relatives plus early powered-flight fossils would refute descent from the living gliding groups. An extinct gliding stage with no fossil representative would remain untested.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The membrane extending to the legs can be an adaptation for flight rather than a leftover of gliding.

A gliding ancestor could be extinct and unsampled even if living gliders are not close relatives.

Early bat fossils are few, so locomotor inferences rest on a small sample.
